name: Digital Trust
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Trust Without a Face: The Problem of the Digital Stranger
lesson.summary: Explains how digital interactions strip away the in-person cues that trust normally relies on, why digital copying creates the double-spend problem, and how intermediaries stepped in to solve it at the cost of concentrating risk.
lesson.body:
Every trust mechanism described in the previous chapter, reputation, body language, local courts, physical ID, assumes some shared context between the parties involved. Digital interactions strip most of that context away. When you send money to an account online, click "accept" on a piece of software, or read a review from someone you have never met, you are trusting a party you cannot see, whose history you cannot easily verify, and who may be located anywhere in the world. Digital trust is the set of problems and solutions that arise when human trust has to operate across that gap.

The core technical problem is that digital information is trivially copyable. A physical dollar bill is hard to duplicate convincingly; a digital file representing "one dollar" can be copied perfectly, instantly, and without leaving evidence of the copy. This is known as the double-spend problem: if digital money is just data, what stops someone from spending the same unit twice, once with you and once with someone else, before anyone notices? Physical trust systems never had to solve this, because physical objects cannot occupy two places at once. Digital systems do.

For decades, the answer has been the same one used for stranger-to-stranger trust in the physical world: concentrate trust in an intermediary. A bank keeps the authoritative ledger of who owns what, so that when you pay someone electronically, the bank updates its records and both parties trust that single source of truth rather than trusting each other directly. Payment processors, certificate authorities that vouch for a website's identity, and platforms like online marketplaces that hold funds in escrow all play this role. They do not eliminate the need to trust; they let millions of strangers avoid trusting each other individually by all trusting the same accountable party instead.

This works, but it concentrates risk as well as convenience. If the intermediary is compromised, careless, or dishonest, everyone who relied on it is affected at once. A bank's database can be breached. A certificate authority can be tricked into vouching for a fraudulent website. A platform can freeze funds or go out of business. Digital trust systems built entirely on intermediaries also require that the intermediary's authority be recognized everywhere, which becomes harder as transactions cross borders and legal systems.

This tension, between the convenience of a single trusted party and the risk of depending on it, is the exact problem that later chapters on cryptographic tools and decentralized networks return to again and again. It is worth being clear, in the spirit of a skeptic's guide, that intermediaries are not simply an old-fashioned inconvenience to be engineered away. They provide real services: dispute resolution when something goes wrong, legal recourse, and a single accountable party regulators can hold responsible. Any alternative to intermediary-based digital trust has to actually replace those functions, not just remove the intermediary and hope the problem disappears with it.

Before getting there, it helps to understand how digital systems are actually connected to each other, which is the subject of the next few chapters.
